newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway unveils robust revised 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Norway unveils robust revised 1997 budget.

text.p: Oil-rich Norway presented a revised 1997 national budget on Tuesday with a soaring surplus and an upgraded forecast for gross domestic product (GDP) growth.

The revised budget, which confirmed Norway's economy is among the strongest in Europe, put overall GDP growth at 3.9 percent, up from 3.1 percent in a forecast made when the budget was adopted by parliament in December.
The mainland GDP, which excludes the thriving offshore oil and gas sector, was seen to rise 3.3 percent, up from 2.5 percent in the previous forecast.
The budget surplus, which will be ploughed into the State Petroleum Fund for investment in securities abroad, was forecast at 57.3 billion crowns, up from 55.4 billion.
The consumer price growth forecast was left unchanged at 2.5 percent from December.

"The growth in the Norwegian economy is continuing. With an average increase of mainland GDP of 3.6 percent over the last four years, the economy is now operating close to capacity," the Finance Ministry said in a statement.
It attributed the increase to more private consumption and an upswing in fixed investments in the petroleum sector.
Central Bank Governor Kjell Storvik last week renewed a call for the fiscal budget to be tighter.The central bank is concerned with longer-term inflation.

Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg, while saying that booming property prices provided a warning signal, said the austerity measures to keep the economy from overheating had already been taken in December.
"Now we are only trying to carry out the cooling-down steps adopted in December," he said. "The revised budget is not a new budget but a way of monitoring how things are going."
Despite the surplus projected for this year, the government said last year it will keep a tight grip on the money purse for fear of fuelling inflation.
Stoltenberg denied that the government refrained from proposing additional cuts because it is an election year.
Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland's Labour minority government, which has lost support in recent opinion polls, faces elections in September.
Oystein Stephansen, head of economic research at S-E Banken in Oslo, said the revised budget "confirmed that Norway's economy is sailing along with good growth".

"But there are warning signals such as the strong rise in property prices, increasing credit growth and solid growth in private consumption. These show the need to tighten fiscal policy in 1998 after the election," Stephansen said.
The ministry noted with satisfaction that the Norwegian crown had weakened recently and was approaching the exchange rate levels it had late last year prior to rallying in January.
The ministry said unemployment -- a major election issue for the government -- had been reduced from over six percent to close to four percent of the labour force in the period 1994-97.
Wage settlements have been moderate so far this year, indicating a wage growth from 1996 to 1997 at approximately 3.5 percent, or one percent taking estimated inflation into account.
"This is a clear deceleration compared to the close to three percent growth in 1996, which was the highest real wage increase since the 1970s," the ministry said.

During the 1990s Norway's current account surplus has been steadily increasing thanks to rising petroleum exports. The surplus is estimated at 81.3 billion crowns in 1997, compared to 72.9 billion last year.
